cards.name: Lantern of Verbs
cards.example: The lantern lit the path.
notes: Present: I light the lantern.
Past: I lit the lantern.
Perfect: I have lit the lantern.
cards.tip: Three forms. One little light.

cards.name: Pumpkin Comparisons
cards.example: This pumpkin is bigger.
notes: dark → darker → darkest
big → bigger → biggest
This is the biggest pumpkin.
cards.tip: Double the final consonant: big → bigger.

cards.name: Ghost of Questions
cards.example: Did the ghost open the door?
notes: Did + person + base verb
Did the ghost open the door?
Yes, it did. / No, it didn't.
cards.tip: After did, use the base verb.

cards.name: The Witch’s Recipe
cards.example: A few pumpkins. A little magic.
notes: A few pumpkins: things we can count.
A little magic: something uncountable.
There are a few pumpkins in the pot.
cards.tip: Count the pumpkins. Feel the magic.

cards.name: Haunted Prepositions
cards.example: The bat is above the gate.
notes: The cat is between the pumpkins.
The ghost is behind the tree.
The bat is above the gate.
cards.tip: Tiny words tell us where things are.

cards.name: Blood Moon Story
cards.example: I was reading when the moon turned red.
notes: I was reading.
They were walking.
An action was in progress in the past.
cards.tip: Set the scene. Then tell the story.

cards.name: The Star
cards.example: TWINKLE, twinkle, little star,
notes: TWINKLE, twinkle, little star,
How I wonder what you are !
Star and are share the same ending sound.
cards.tip: Read a real nursery poem aloud.

source.author: Jane Taylor
excerptLines: How I wonder what you are !
source.rights: Public-domain original text; source transcription credited
source.authorNote: The linked transcription credits Ann and Jane Taylor jointly. The Morgan Library attributes this poem to Jane Taylor.

cards.name: The Owl and the Pussy-Cat
cards.example: And hand in hand, on the edge of the sand,
notes: And hand in hand, on the edge of the sand,
They danced by the light of the moon,
Hand and sand rhyme inside the same line.
cards.tip: Find the rhyme within the line.

source.author: Edward Lear
excerptLines: And hand in hand, on the edge of the sand,
They danced by the light of the moon,
source.rights: Public-domain original text; source transcription credited

cards.name: The Moon
cards.example: The moon has a face like the clock in the hall;
notes: The moon has a face like the clock in the hall;
She shines on thieves on the garden wall,
Hall and wall rhyme. The moon is described as a person.
cards.tip: Notice how a poem gives the moon a face.

source.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
source.location: A Child’s Garden of Verses, opening couplet
excerptLines: The moon has a face like the clock in the hall;
She shines on thieves on the garden wall,
source.rights: Public-domain original text; source transcription credited

cards.name: The Tyger
cards.example: Tyger Tyger, burning bright,
notes: Tyger Tyger, burning bright,
In the forests of the night;
Bright and night rhyme. Tyger is an older spelling of tiger.
cards.tip: Listen for the repeated b in burning bright.

source.author: William Blake
excerptLines: In the forests of the night;
source.rights: Public-domain original text; source transcription credited

cards.name: Key of Adjectives
cards.example: A brave cat enters a strange house.
notes: Adjectives describe nouns.
A bright lantern. A strange noise.
The brave cat opens the gate.
cards.tip: Find three adjectives in your next story.

cards.name: Footsteps in the Past
cards.example: The keeper walked home.
notes: Present: I walk past the gate.
Past: I walked past the gate.
Perfect: I have walked past the gate.
cards.tip: Regular verbs often end in -ed.

cards.name: The Talking Pumpkin
cards.example: This pumpkin can tell a story.
notes: Can + base verb describes ability.
The pumpkin can speak English.
It cannot fly, but it can sing.
cards.tip: Use can without to.

cards.name: Time for Tea
cards.example: We meet on Monday at night.
notes: At night. In October. On Monday.
Use on with days.
We read in the evening.
cards.tip: Small time words make a big difference.

cards.name: Better Late Than Never
cards.example: The ghost arrived late, but arrived.
notes: Doing something late can be better than not doing it.
The ghost was late for reading club.
It joined in instead of giving up.
cards.tip: A traditional proverb about making an effort.

cards.name: Two Heads Are Better
cards.key: TWO HEADS ARE BETTER THAN ONE
cards.example: Two friends solve the puzzle together.
notes: Working together can help us find better ideas.
One ghost reads. One checks the words.
Together they understand the story.
cards.tip: A traditional proverb about teamwork.

cards.name: Practice Makes Perfect
cards.example: The witch practises a little each day.
notes: Practice helps us improve a skill.
The witch reads five new words each day.
A mistake is a chance to practise again.
cards.tip: A traditional proverb about steady practice.

cards.name: A Friend in Need
cards.key: A FRIEND IN NEED IS A FRIEND INDEED
cards.example: A friend brings a lantern to help.
notes: A true friend helps when things are difficult.
The path was dark, so a friend brought a light.
Indeed means really or truly.
cards.tip: A traditional proverb about friendship.

cards.name: The Hidden Key
cards.example: The key is under the old book.
notes: The key is under the book.
The lock is next to the gate.
A note is inside the box.
cards.tip: Describe a hiding place in English.

cards.name: Slow and Steady
cards.key: SLOW AND STEADY WINS THE RACE
cards.example: A little progress every day adds up.
notes: Calm, regular effort can bring success.
The tortoise learns one new word a day.
It keeps going, even when learning is slow.
cards.tip: A traditional proverb about patience.

cards.name: Who Has Seen the Wind?
cards.example: Who has seen the wind?
notes: Who has seen the wind?
Neither I nor you:
But when the leaves hang trembling,
The wind is passing through.
You and through rhyme, although their spellings differ.
cards.tip: Read the stanza and listen for you / through.

source.author: Christina Rossetti
excerptLines: But when the leaves hang trembling,
source.rights: Public-domain original text; source transcription credited

cards.name: Quiet as a Mouse
cards.example: The reader is as quiet as a mouse.
notes: A simile compares two things.
As quiet as a mouse means very quiet.
The mouse listens beside the book.
cards.tip: Use as + adjective + as to compare.

cards.name: The Silver Lining
cards.key: EVERY CLOUD HAS A SILVER LINING
cards.example: Even a difficult day can hold something good.
notes: A difficult situation may have a good side.
The rain kept us inside.
We found a new story to read together.
cards.tip: A traditional proverb about finding hope.

cards.name: Beyond the Cover
cards.key: DON’T JUDGE A BOOK BY ITS COVER
cards.example: An old cover can hide a wonderful story.
notes: Appearance does not tell us everything.
The book looked old and dusty.
Inside was a funny, exciting story.
cards.tip: A traditional proverb about looking deeper.

cards.name: Actions Speak Louder
cards.example: The keeper helps instead of just promising.
notes: What we do can matter more than what we say.
The keeper said he would help.
Then he carried the books home.
cards.tip: A traditional proverb about keeping promises.

cards.name: Birds of a Feather
cards.key: BIRDS OF A FEATHER FLOCK TOGETHER
cards.example: Friends often share interests.
notes: People with similar interests often spend time together.
The night readers all enjoy ghost stories.
They meet at the library every Friday.
cards.tip: A traditional proverb about shared interests.

cards.name: Peter Piper’s Practice
cards.example: Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers,
notes: Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers,
Repeat the p sound slowly. A peck is an old measure.
cards.tip: A traditional tongue twister, recited by our skeleton.

source.author: Traditional
excerptLines: Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers,
source.rights: Public-domain original text; source transcription credited

cards.name: The Witches’ Chant
cards.example: Double, double toil and trouble;
notes: Double, double toil and trouble;
Fire burn, and cauldron bubble.
Trouble and bubble rhyme. Toil means hard work.
cards.tip: Say the witches’ chant with a steady beat.

source.author: William Shakespeare
source.rights: Public-domain original text; source transcription credited

cards.name: Fortune Favours the Brave
cards.example: The learner tries a new story.
notes: Trying something difficult can lead to good things.
The learner felt shy but read the first line.
One brave step made the next step easier.
cards.tip: A traditional proverb about trying.

cards.name: Knowledge Is Power
cards.example: New words open new doors.
notes: Learning helps us understand and do more.
The reader learnt the meaning of a sign.
Now the hidden door makes sense.
cards.tip: A traditional proverb about the value of learning.

cards.name: Empire State after Dark
cards.example: A frightfully tall hello from New York!
notes: The supplied photograph becomes a Halloween postcard.
Compare heights using taller than.
The back is a little postcard to the night readers.
cards.tip: A photographic print on a real, thin 3D postcard.

reference.note: Halloween transformation of supplied photo; new postcard text.

cards.name: Manhattan after Dark
cards.example: Wish you were here… if you dare.
notes: A blood moon rises over the supplied Manhattan view.
The skyline is glowing. The water is reflecting the lights.
City words: skyline, harbour, pier and mist.
cards.tip: Describe what you can see in the picture.

reference.note: Halloween transformation of supplied photo; new postcard text.

cards.name: The Midnight Focus
cards.example: The witch who lives next door is friendly.
notes: The original Focus box is printed unchanged.
Halloween examples are added beneath the original box.
Who refers to people; which refers to things.
cards.tip: Look for the relative clause in each new sentence.

reference.note: Original source box unchanged; separate Halloween examples added.

cards.name: Two Ways to Say Boo
cards.example: My favourite colour is orange.
notes: The original British/American table is printed unchanged.
New Halloween examples appear below it in two columns.
Our neighbour gives us biscuits. Our neighbor gives us cookies.
cards.tip: Same Halloween, different English.

reference.note: Original source box unchanged; separate Halloween examples added.

cards.name: Become, Go or Grow?
cards.example: The pumpkin became a lantern.
notes: The original German werden table is printed unchanged.
Become can introduce a noun: became a lantern.
Go bad and grow darker describe changes of state.
cards.tip: Choose the English verb that fits the meaning.

reference.note: Original image printed unchanged; separate Halloween learning prompts added.

cards.name: Spooky Sounds
cards.example: A creepy night celebration.
notes: The original spelling and pronunciation table is unchanged.
The Halloween words extend the four spelling patterns.
The original phonetic symbols stay in their source image.
cards.tip: Read the word groups aloud and compare the sounds.

reference.note: Original image printed unchanged; separate Halloween learning prompts added.

cards.name: The Midnight Map
cards.example: Canada is north of the USA.
notes: The supplied map and vocabulary panel are printed unchanged.
Country labels, borders and the map itself are preserved.
Only the extra ghost-trail sentence is an invented story.
cards.tip: Use the source map to practise directions.

reference.note: Original image printed unchanged; separate Halloween learning prompts added.

cards.topic: A poem from the supplied textbook
cards.example: Read the original bird poem aloud.
notes: The supplied original poem and picture are printed unchanged.
The author is not named in the supplied extract.
The added reading prompts are not extra lines of the poem.
cards.tip: Read the original aloud and find its rhyming pairs.

cards.name: Haunted Definitions
cards.key: A PERSON WHO · A THING WHICH
cards.example: Do you know the person who carved this pumpkin?
notes: The supplied picture strip and original exercise are unchanged.
The new Halloween sentences are extra examples.
No answers are inserted into the original exercise.
cards.tip: A person who …; a thing which …

cards.name: As Spooky as …
cards.example: My pumpkin is as big as yours.
notes: The original as … as Focus box is printed unchanged.
The added sentences compare pumpkins, lights and houses.
The adjective stays in its base form between as and as.
cards.tip: Use as … as for equality; not as … as for a difference.

reference.note: Original image printed unchanged; separate Halloween learning prompts added.

cards.name: Towers after Dark
cards.example: Which tower is the tallest in the diagram?
notes: The original text and height diagram are printed unchanged.
The comparison refers to the supplied diagram and its values.
The pumpkin tower is a fictional extra example.
cards.tip: Compare the heights shown in the original diagram.

reference.note: Original image printed unchanged; separate Halloween learning prompts added.

cards.name: Highlight 8 · Halloween Edition
cards.example: A legendary cover for a season of stories.
notes: The Highlight 8 Halloween cover is also a collectible card.
The front is the almanac cover; the back carries the driving-you-batty meme.
This is the only Legendary card in Season I.
cards.tip: The almanac cover and the collectible share their artwork.

reference.note: Existing edited book artwork reused for the almanac cover and collectible card.

cards.name: Bloody Friday
cards.example: School has finished. This card, regrettably, has not. Put the kettle on; Friday is now a limited edition.
notes: School has finished. This card, regrettably, has not. Put the kettle on; Friday is now a limited edition.
Move your imaginary weekend one dramatic step away.
Gain +2 Patience and a suspiciously cold cup of tea.
I’m a detention card with a weekend-shaped identity crisis.
cards.tip: Imaginary card effects · British humour

cards.example: A thrilling sequel in which the school rules are copied out by hand. Every sentence has somehow survived the first reading.
notes: A thrilling sequel in which the school rules are copied out by hand. Every sentence has somehow survived the first reading.
Copy one imaginary paragraph.
Gain +3 Handwriting; lose one pen to the void.
My replay value is mostly stationery.

cards.name: Verweis
cards.example: Official displeasure, now available in premium parchment. The envelope would like a quiet word.
notes: Official displeasure, now available in premium parchment. The envelope would like a quiet word.
Place one Very Serious Stamp.
All nearby imaginary paperwork becomes 10% more official.
I’m a rectangle that has learned to sound disappointed.

cards.name: Verschärfter Verweis für Vapen
cards.example: The sequel arrived in a cloud of remarkably poor judgement. Even the Halloween fog machine has raised an eyebrow.
notes: The sequel arrived in a cloud of remarkably poor judgement. Even the Halloween fog machine has raised an eyebrow.
Clear the imaginary fog.
Gain +2 Fresh Air; summon one Extremely Formal Envelope.
I’ve been upgraded. This is rarely good news for a piece of paper.

cards.topic: One small line. So much lore.
cards.example: One tiny line. An astonishing amount of lore. The homework is, of course, in the other bag.

Add one imaginary tally.
Draw an Excuse; if it says “the other bag”, draw another.
I contain fewer pixels than the explanation I’m about to receive.

cards.example: A brief cooling-off intermission, presented with the production values of an arctic expedition.
notes: A brief cooling-off intermission, presented with the production values of an arctic expedition.
Pause the imaginary drama for one turn.
Gain +2 Composure and a dignified penguin.
I’ve turned a short break into an entire character arc.

cards.example: An academically rigorous assessment consisting of four words and a long, theatrical exhale.
notes: An academically rigorous assessment consisting of four words and a long, theatrical exhale.
All imaginary tasks become “a bit much” for one turn.
Gain +2 Dramatic Sighs and one raised eyebrow.
I’m self-aware enough to suspect I’m being pronounced wrong.
